accuracy.reason: All eight objectives are accurately bounded: discovery, delegated lookup, records, TTL, negative responses, steering, diagnosis and trust. Source audit and both diagram meanings agree.

evidence.quote: That validates DNS data, not the Notes application. DNSSEC does not encrypt the query, certify service health or guarantee availability. Unsigned data does not gain these signature checks merely because a resolver supports DNSSEC.

mechanisms.reason: Actors, referrals, alias continuation, independently aged caches and separate health policy make successful and failed operations traceable.

evidence.quote: Assume empty relevant caches in our teaching hierarchy. The recursive resolver asks root, receives a referral to .example, asks that authority, then follows its referral to the notes.example authority. That authority holds the final records for api.notes.example. Root does not hold every host's address.

coherence.reason: Names and caches precede resolvers and records; the same Notes lookup develops into moves, outages and validation without missing required prerequisites.

evidence.quote: Now consider a direct address record for api.notes.example instead of the alias. TTL, or time to live, limits ordinary cache reuse in seconds. Each cache ages the TTL it received; it is not a worldwide update timer.

decisions.reason: Short TTL trades refresh cost and DNS dependence for faster ordinary changes; overlap, monitoring, failover capacity and separate diagnosis guide decisions.

evidence.quote: Shorter TTLs mean more refresh queries and more frequent dependence on working DNS. Independent caches and connection lifetimes prevent a simultaneous cutover. Some resolvers can even serve expired data when refreshing fails, so TTL is not a hard global recovery deadline.

clarity.reason: Definitions and concrete times make the lesson usable; eight dense cards and the packed final security card require careful reading, but no required concept is left undefined.

evidence.quote: IPv4 and IPv6 are two IP address families. An A record supplies an IPv4 address, such as 192.0.2.10. An AAAA record supplies an IPv6 address, such as 2001:db8::10. A client uses an address family it can reach.

outcomes.reason: C1–2: learner separates hostname discovery, connection and HTTPS path and denies health assurance. C3–5: defines stub/resolver/authority/zone/delegation, follows both referrals, and explains cache shortcuts. C6–8: A/AAAA address families and CNAME target resolution/separate caching are taught and quoted. These cover card objectives 1–3; their definitions are explicit on slides 1–3.

C1: learner correctly transfers the timeline to 12:59. C2: lowers TTL early, waits old lifetime, retains both destinations and monitors traffic/errors/connections. C3: explains refresh/dependency costs and independent caches, connections and stale serving. Slide 4 supports every element and its objective.

C1: cached negative answer retains its own lifetime despite new positive TTL. C2: NXDOMAIN and requested-type NODATA distinguished. C3: SERVFAIL is resolution failure, may be cached and is not absence proof. All supported by exact slide 5 quotes; negative-answer objective covered.

C1: separate health signal/policy changes returned destinations. C2: shared caches and repeated connection requests explain unequal traffic. C3: cached east and open connections prevent instant movement. C4: west needs health, reachability and capacity. Slide 6 quotations support all and its objective.

C1: cached addresses/open sessions explain continued access. C2: inspect recursive name/type/status/TTL then authoritative records/delegation. C3: connection/HTTPS and HTTP 500 handled separately. C4: redundancy cannot fix common configuration or application failure. Slide 7 supports each; slide 5 supplies the missing-data versus failure distinction.

C1: signature chain establishes DNS origin/integrity. C2: no query encryption or health proof. C3: HTTPS certificate authenticates requested api.notes.example and encrypts HTTP even with an alias. Exact slide 8 evidence supports all and the trust objective.

sourceChecks.claim: Live Cloudflare lookup sequence separates address discovery from later HTTP and explains cached answers; supports slide 1.
Live AWS route sequence follows resolver to root/TLD/authority, caches delegations and returns address before web traffic; supports illustrative hierarchy and role separation.
Live AWS record reference defines A IPv4, AAAA IPv6 and CNAME name mapping; RFC 1034 resolution algorithm confirms separate CNAME caching and continuation to target.

RFC 8767 defines ordinary TTL reuse and permits stale data when refresh fails; RFC 1034 describes aging cached records. Timeline, lack of push replacement, and non-global deadline follow; connection lifetime is outside DNS.
RFC 9520 separates absent data from failed resolution, references distinct negative-response TTL and requires failure caching; adding positive data does not reset a resolver cache.

AWS explicitly configures health checks and selects DNS responses using health. Cache reuse from AWS routing/RFC 1034 explains why query shares are not request shares and removed answers do not migrate connections; health/capacity remain separate.
RFC 1034 resolver algorithm checks cached data, follows delegation and tries other servers on failure; these dependencies explain cache reuse, redundancy limitations and separate service diagnosis.

RFC 4033 establishes data-origin authentication/integrity, trust-anchor chains and no confidentiality or service-health validation. Supplementary live RFC 9525 (https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9525.html), sections 6.1.1–6.1.2, confirms HTTPS reference identity is the original URL hostname and intermediate DNS names do not replace it. DNSSEC does not replace HTTPS identity checks.
